outcome: No resolution found: the problem is still listed as open (erdosproblems.com #242, last edited 7 May 2026; Wikipedia, last edited 3 Aug 2026). Since 26 Jan 2024 the record holds a computational extension to 10^18, several partial or conjectural frameworks, and three unrefereed claims of a full or prime-case proof (Dyachenko Nov 2025; Bradford Feb 2026; Chen Aug 2026), none accepted by any reader I could identify; the Bradford text itself calls its argument an outline and its covering step is not carried out.
problem_asks: Statement as given (Wikipedia, Jan 2024): for every integer n ≥ 2 there exist positive integers x, y, z with 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. Parts: (a) the universal claim over every n ≥ 2, which has infinitely many instances, so no finite check settles it; (b) for each such n, the existence of at least one triple; (c) the triple is of positive integers, with no distinctness requirement in this wording. Reduction noted in the sources (not part of the statement): if p is prime and 4/p has a solution, then 4/(kp) has one by scaling every denominator by k, so the prime case carries the whole problem. Wording difference: erdosproblems.com #242 asks for distinct 1 ≤ x < y < z and states n > 2. Distinct triples cannot exist for n = 2 (the largest sum of three distinct unit fractions is 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 < 2), so the two wordings differ at n = 2 only. The record matches the Wikipedia wording.

events.what_happened: Obláth (1950), a brute-force search reported by Wikipedia as verifying the conjecture for n ≤ 10^5 (Wikipedia gives the paper as written 1948, published 1950). The primary paper was not located or opened; the venue is not checked.
events.delivers: Finite check: the conjecture holds for every n ≤ 10^5. A finite check of a universal claim moves no quantity the problem asks for.
events.remains: Every n > 10^5.
events.directly_checkable: Each n is a finite search for x, y, z; any single n can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; no counterexample reported.

events.what_happened: Mordell's polynomial identities settle the conjecture for every n outside six residue classes mod 840: 1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529 (the squares 1², 11², 13², 17², 19², 23²). Wikipedia dates this to 1967; erdosproblems.com cites Mordell as [Mo68] in a forum comment and as [Mo69] on the problem page, so the year is uncertain within 1967 to 1969. The primary paper was not opened. Wikipedia and the forum both say 1009 is the smallest prime in an uncovered class (1009 = 840 + 169).
events.delivers: A three-term solution for every n not congruent to 1, 121, 169, 289, 361 or 529 (mod 840), per the sources' summaries. This covers all but six residue classes out of 840.
events.remains: Every n ≡ 1, 121, 169, 289, 361 or 529 (mod 840), including the prime 1009.
events.directly_checkable: Identities are explicit polynomial families; instances can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Partial; cuts toward the conjecture by covering a large residue set.

events.what_happened: Vaughan (1970), a result on almost all n, cited as a much stronger 'almost all' result by Thomas Bloom on the erdosproblems.com forum (1 Feb 2026) and listed as Va70 on the problem page. A forum comment (Alfaiz, 23 Nov 2025) gives an exception bound of the form N / exp(c (log N)^(2/3)). Wikipedia also cites Webb (1970) and Vaughan (1970) on the sparseness of counterexamples. The primary paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Per the forum and Wikipedia: the representation exists for all but a sparse set of n. The forum gives an exception-count bound of the form N / exp(c (log N)^(2/3)). Whether that count is over all n or over primes is not verified.
events.remains: The exceptional set is not shown empty. The bound does not give existence for every n.
events.doubts: Primary not read. The object the exception bound counts (all n or primes) is not verified, so the quantity it moves cannot be stated with confidence.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture (sparseness of exceptions); does not settle it.

events.what_happened: Allan Swett's computer check of the conjecture for n up to 10^14, about 150 hours, using a sieve on a single modular equation. Reported in the abstract of Salez (2014); MathWorld and OEIS state the same bound in search snippets (not opened). Swett's own report was not located.
events.delivers: Finite check: the conjecture holds for all n ≤ 10^14. A finite check moves no quantity the problem asks for.
events.remains: Every n > 10^14.
events.directly_checkable: Computer search; each n is checkable by hand.
events.doubts: Primary not located; the bound comes from secondary reports. Salez's abstract says N = 10^14 while OEIS says n < 10^14 (search snippets), a boundary difference that does not matter here.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; no counterexample reported.

events.what_happened: Elsholtz and Tao, 'Counting the number of solutions to the Erdős-Straus equation on unit fractions' (arXiv:1107.1010): studies f(n), the number of solutions to 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z, and restates the conjecture as f(n) > 0 for all n ≥ 2. Reduces to primes. Publishes bounds on sums of f(p) over primes. Journal reference: J. Aust. Math. Soc. 94 (2013), 50–105.
events.revisions: v1 6 Jul 2011; v2 8 Jul 2011; v3 29 Jul 2011; v4 26 May 2012; v5 23 Oct 2012; v6 2 Aug 2015 (corrects an error in the statement and proof of Theorem 1.9 and adds references). Published J. Aust. Math. Soc. 94 (2013).
events.delivers: Counting, not existence: N log²N ≪ Σ_{p ≤ N} f(p) ≪ N log²N log log N (per abstract); f(p) = O(log³p · log log p) for a subset of primes of density arbitrarily close to 1; f(p) ≪ p^(3/5) + O(1/log log p) for all primes p (per abstract). A typical prime has few solutions. No n is shown to have f(n) > 0.
events.remains: Existence of at least one solution for every n.

checked_by.who: Referees of J. Aust. Math. Soc.
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published (2013), per the journal reference on the arXiv page

events.direction: Counting result; neither proves nor refutes existence for any given n.

events.what_happened: Ionascu and Wilson (2011), named in Wikipedia's list of dated references. Not opened and no title or content found; included so the record shows it was seen.
events.delivers: Not established: the primary was not read.
events.remains: Not established.
events.doubts: Not opened, so no scope is recorded.
events.direction: Not established.

events.what_happened: Salez, 'The Erdős-Straus conjecture: New modular equations and checking up to N=10^17' (arXiv:1406.6307, single version, 24 Jun 2014): proves a complete set of seven modular equations (three of them new) and uses them in an optimised sieve. A C++ program checks the conjecture for all n ≤ 10^17, taking minutes at 10^14 and about 16 hours at 10^17 on a typical computer.
events.delivers: Finite verification to 10^17, and congruence identities that cover residue classes. A finite check moves no quantity the problem asks for.
events.remains: Every n > 10^17.
events.directly_checkable: The C++ program is an ancillary file on arXiv (per the abstract page); the modular equations can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; no counterexample reported.

events.what_happened: Ionascu and Bradford, 'A Geometric Consideration of the Erdős-Straus Conjecture' (arXiv:1411.3403, per the search URL ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1411.3403; the year is from the arXiv identifier). A later 'geometric reduction' paper by Bradford is listed in a university repository. Neither was opened.
events.delivers: Not established: the paper was not read.
events.remains: Not established.
events.doubts: Not opened, so no scope is recorded.
events.direction: Not established.

events.what_happened: Bradford, 'A note on the Erdő-Straus Conjecture' (arXiv:1906.00561): assumes that a prime p has a solution x ≤ y ≤ z, and shows that under that assumption z is determined by x, y and p, so the problem reduces by one variable. The abstract does not claim a proof of the conjecture. A 2026 paper, seen only in a search snippet, lists it as published in Integers 21 (2021), #A24.
events.revisions: v1 3 Jun 2019; v2 2 Mar 2020 (current; 11 pages, 2 figures).
events.delivers: A conditional reduction only: it assumes the existence it would need to prove, so it establishes no case of the conjecture.
events.remains: Everything: the reduction starts from the conjecture's own assumption for each prime.
events.direction: Reformulation; no direction on existence.

events.what_happened: Bright and Loughran, 'Brauer-Manin obstruction for Erdős-Straus surfaces' (arXiv:1908.02526, v1 7 Aug 2019, v2 12 May 2020; Bull. London Math. Soc. 2020 per DOI on the arXiv page). They study the integral Hasse principle and strong approximation for the Erdős-Straus equation, treated as integer points on a family of surfaces, and show a Brauer-Manin obstruction. The abstract does not state whether the conjecture is proved. Search snippets say Theorem 1.9 concerns non-density of the relevant map; the full text was not read.
events.revisions: v1 7 Aug 2019 (17 pages); v2 12 May 2020; published Bull. London Math. Soc. (2020), DOI 10.1112/blms.12374 per the arXiv page.
events.delivers: A statement about strong approximation and the integral Hasse principle on the surfaces, a neighbouring question. It does not establish that a solution exists for each n.
events.remains: The conjecture itself, which the abstract does not claim to settle.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published (2020) per the DOI on the arXiv page; not verified on the journal site

events.direction: A different question (approximation on the surfaces); does not cut for or against existence for individual n.

events.what_happened: Gionfriddo and Guardo, 'A short proof of the conjecture of Erdős-Straus for every n ≡ 13 mod 24' (arXiv:2005.03273): explicit x, y, z for every n ≡ 13 (mod 24). v3 is titled 'A new and short proof' (per a search snippet). Journal reference: J. Interdisciplinary Math., published online 23 June 2021 (per the comments field).
events.revisions: v1 7 May 2020; v2 23 Aug 2020; v3 24 Aug 2021 (current).
events.delivers: Complete for the residue class n ≡ 13 (mod 24) (explicit triples). Does not treat other classes. Per a search snippet, the authors say the class n ≡ 1 (mod 24) still needs handling.
events.remains: Every n outside n ≡ 13 (mod 24), including n ≡ 1 (mod 24).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published online 23 June 2021, per the comments field

events.directly_checkable: Explicit triples for each n in the class can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Partial; cuts toward the conjecture (one residue class).

events.what_happened: Lopez, 'Structure and form of the solutions of the Erdős-Straus conjecture' (arXiv:2206.10319, single author): classifies solutions of the form (du, dv, duv), gives characterisations for some primes including p = 1009, studies solutions with gcd(x,y,z) = x, and classifies cases in which two variables coincide. The abstract does not claim a proof of the conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 16 Jun 2022; v2 21 Nov 2022; v3 10 Dec 2022; v4 20 Aug 2024 (current, 12 pages). The v4 revision falls inside the window; this event is dated to the first version.
events.delivers: Classifications of special solution shapes and characterisations for some individual primes. Does not establish existence for any class of n.
events.remains: Existence for every n.
events.direction: Structural; no direction on existence.

events.what_happened: Bradford, 'Elemental Patterns from the Erdős Straus Conjecture' (arXiv:2403.16047, posted 24 Mar 2024). Conjectures that for every prime p there is an integer x with ⌈p/4⌉ ≤ x ≤ ⌈p/2⌉ and a divisor d of x² satisfying one of two congruences modulo (4x − p). The abstract says the solutions of these congruences correspond one-to-one with solutions of the Erdős-Straus equation. Published in Integers 25 (2025), #A54 (received 25 Jul 2024, accepted 19 May 2025, published 27 Jun 2025, per search snippets; the journal PDF was not parseable).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (24 Mar 2024, 17 KB). Journal version Integers 25 (2025) #A54 per search snippets.
events.delivers: An equivalence (claimed proved in the abstract) between the modular solutions and Erdős-Straus solutions. The existence of such x for every prime is conjectured, not proved, so no n is settled.
events.remains: The conjectured existence for every prime, and hence the conjecture.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted 19 May 2025 and published 27 Jun 2025, per search snippets of the journal PDF; the PDF itself was not parseable

events.directly_checkable: The divisor and congruence conditions for a given prime p can be checked by hand.
events.direction: A reformulation with an equivalence; the existence conjecture for primes is open.

events.what_happened: Lopez, 'A Complete Congruence System for the Erdős-Straus Conjecture' (arXiv:2404.01508, single author, v1 1 Apr 2024, v3 15 Apr 2024). Defines a congruence system 'for which there are always solutions' (abstract wording) and two new solution types, A and B. Conjectures that the system includes all primes and that every prime has a Type A or Type B solution.
events.revisions: v1 1 Apr 2024; v2 3 Apr 2024; v3 15 Apr 2024 (current, 19 pages).
events.delivers: Conditional and conjectural: the coverage of all primes by Types A and B is conjectured in the abstract, not proved. The abstract does not claim to resolve the conjecture.
events.remains: The conjectured coverage of all primes, and so the conjecture.
events.direction: Conjectural framework; no direction on existence beyond the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Schuh, 'The Erdős-Straus Conjecture and Pythagorean Primes' (arXiv:2503.11672, math.GM, single version 26 Feb 2025): restricts to Pythagorean primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4), splits the equation into two Diophantine equations, and states two conjectures on representations of such primes, supported by empirical evidence. Gives a plausibility argument for one and an algorithm for finding a, b, c.
events.delivers: Conjectures only, per the abstract. Nothing is proved.
events.remains: Everything.
events.doubts: The conjectures rest on empirical evidence and a plausibility argument; the posting is in math.GM and has no review that I could find.
events.direction: Conjectural; toward the conjecture only in the sense of a proposed representation for each prime of the stated form.

events.what_happened: Mballa, 'Partial Resolution of the Erdős-Straus, Sierpiński, and Generalized Erdős-Straus Conjectures Using New Analytical Formulas' (arXiv:2502.20935, sole author). Gives two analytical formulas. The first rests on a divisibility condition; the second relies on a perfect-square conjecture: that t²(4x − n)² − 2ntx is a perfect square for some positive t, x, for every n ≥ 2. The abstract calls the method a partial resolution that 'opens the way to a complete proof'.
events.revisions: v1 28 Feb 2025 (26 KB); v2 16 Feb 2026 (29 KB, current).
events.delivers: Explicit solutions for a subset of n given by the first formula; the subset is not characterised in the abstract. The second formula is conditional on the perfect-square conjecture, which the abstract states as a conjecture.
events.remains: Every n outside the explicit subset, and the perfect-square conjecture.
events.directly_checkable: The explicit formulas can be checked for a given n.
events.doubts: Two preprints by Hassan Bouamoud on Preprints.org disagree on the perfect-square question. The first (Dec 2025; DOI 10.20944/preprints202512.2732.v1) argues the polynomial does not always give a square for n = 3. The second (Jan 2026) claims that for every n ≥ 2 there are t, x making it a square. Both are unrefereed; the search snippets show their titles and abstracts only, and the preprints were not opened.
events.direction: Partial, toward the conjecture for a subset; conditional on an unproved square-existence statement.

events.what_happened: Dyachenko (listed as 'Eduard Dyachenko V', independent researcher), 'Constructive Proofs of the Erdős-Straus Conjecture for Prime Numbers of the Form P ≡ 1 (mod 4)' (arXiv:2511.07465, single version, 7 Nov 2025). The abstract says that for every prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4) there is a representation 4/P = 1/A + 1/(bP) + 1/(cP), with (δ, b, c) built explicitly by a method (ED2) that solves a linear system; the central result is Theorem 10.21. Also introduces 'convolution' and 'anti-convolution' transformations and reports computation.
events.revisions: v1 only (7 Nov 2025, 98 KB).
events.delivers: As claimed in the abstract: for every prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4), a three-term representation. Read with the other cases, this would settle the conjecture: primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) follow from the identity 4/n = 1/((n+1)/4) + 1/(n(n+1)/4) (my derivation; both denominators are integers when n ≡ 3 mod 4), p = 2 is immediate, and the standard reduction covers composite n. But the text as read limits what is proved (see doubts), so the delivered scope is unresolved.
events.remains: On the Conclusion as read, the general case with P ranging over infinite sets is 'certainly not proven constructively in the present work', and the Appendix D sections that use Dirichlet's theorem and finite coverings are 'conditional in nature'; for a fixed odd prime P, the existence of a solution is 'strictly proven'. Whether the uniform statement for all P ≡ 1 (mod 4) is established is therefore open on the text read.
events.directly_checkable: Each prime's triple can be checked by hand. Section 10 gives computed examples, per the extraction read (P = 2521, 3529).
events.doubts: (1) The Conclusion, as extracted by WebFetch, restricts the proof to fixed primes and calls the infinite-family argument conditional (see remains). The extraction is a summary, not the verbatim text, so this needs a direct reading. (2) Remark 9.4, as extracted, says the lattice-counting theorems 'by themselves do not guarantee the existence of solutions to the nonlinear identity' and that 'an external input is required'. (3) Section 9.13 is titled 'Anticonvolution for 11 and the Canon Existence Hypothesis', which suggests a hypothesis, not a proof, at that step. (4) The proof of Theorem 9.2 is informal ('Due to the uniformity of the distribution and the constancy of the lattice index, the average time to success is bounded'), with no supporting argument in the extract. (5) Several lemmas defer their proofs to Appendix D, some with proof sketches only, one in Russian. (6) Section 10 is computational tables, which check examples and prove nothing for all primes. (7) Single author, unaffiliated, no journal, and no public review found. (8) On 18 Nov 2025 Thomas Bloom said on the erdosproblems.com forum that none of the claimed proofs he had looked at 'have seemed credible'; the forum text read does not name the papers, so I cannot say whether this paper is among them.
events.direction: Cuts toward the conjecture: claims existence for each prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4).
events.object: No counterexample. The claimed object is a family of explicit triples: for each prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4), a parameter triple (δ, b, c) gives 4/P = 1/A + 1/(bP) + 1/(cP). The construction (ED2) is described as explicit, but the Conclusion as extracted says the existence for infinitely many P is not proved constructively, so explicitness and existence for every prime are separate questions in this text.

events.what_happened: Ghermoul, 'Exact Polynomial Families Solving the Erdős-Straus Equation' (arXiv:2508.07383, single author, 10 Aug 2025). Four polynomials p1 to p4 in x, y, z ≥ 1. Inserting the first three into a = 4 p_i + 1 gives values of a with explicit solutions. The author conjectures the four families together cover every a ≡ 1 (mod 4), supported by computation up to q = 10^9, and says the case a ≡ 1 (mod 4) 'remains the central open challenge'.
events.revisions: v1 only (10 Aug 2025).
events.delivers: Explicit solutions for the subset of a ≡ 1 (mod 4) given by the first three families (per the abstract, these 'individually satisfy the conjecture for all their outputs'). The coverage of all a ≡ 1 (mod 4) is conjectural.
events.remains: Every a ≡ 1 (mod 4) outside those families, and the coverage conjecture.
events.directly_checkable: The polynomial identities can be checked for given x, y, z.
events.doubts: Single author, not refereed. The coverage claim is supported only by computation to q = 10^9.
events.direction: Partial, toward the conjecture; coverage conjectural.

events.what_happened: Ghermoul, 'Almost a Complete Proof of the Generalized Erdős-Straus Conjecture: 5/a = 1/b + 1/c + 1/d' (arXiv:2508.07367, 10 Aug 2025). Explicit solutions for 5/a (Sierpiński's variant) for a ≡ 0, 2, 3, 4 (mod 5), and for a = 5q + 1 with q not ≡ 0 (mod 252). The case q ≡ 0 (mod 252) is conjectured via a polynomial p1 and checked computationally to about 10^10 (Mathematica implementation included).
events.revisions: v1 only (10 Aug 2025).
events.delivers: A result for the Sierpiński 5/a problem, not the 4/n problem. For the Erdős-Straus problem it establishes nothing.
events.remains: For 5/a: the case a = 5q + 1 with q ≡ 0 (mod 252), conjectural. For 4/n: not addressed.
events.directly_checkable: Explicit decompositions for given a can be checked by hand.
events.doubts: The title says 'almost a complete proof' and the abstract leaves a subcase conjectural. Single author, not refereed. The erdosproblems.com forum (18 Nov 2025) mentions two papers claiming full or almost complete proofs, one called 'very mistaken' by StijnC; the thread text read does not name them, so this paper's identity in that exchange is unconfirmed.
events.direction: A different problem (5/a), an analogue; settles nothing for 4/n.

events.what_happened: Mihnea and Dumitru (arXiv lists Spiridon Mihnea and Dumitru C. Bogdan), 'Further verification and empirical evidence for the Erdős-Straus conjecture' (arXiv:2509.00128, submitted 29 Aug 2025). Extends Salez's sieve with one more modular filter (a residue set of 2,101,514 classes mod 25,878,772,920), checks the conjecture up to 10^18 (Python for residue generation, C++ with GMP for the rest, in batches, about two weeks on a 'medium setup'), and evaluates the solution-counting function f(p). The abstract describes the result as 'empirical evidence'.
events.revisions: v1 only (29 Aug 2025, 853 KB).
events.delivers: A finite check: no counterexample up to 10^18. The paper calls this empirical evidence, not proof. It also reports data on f(p).
events.remains: Every n > 10^18.
events.directly_checkable: The authors' code is linked from a footnote to github.com/esc-paper/erdos-straus (not opened). The check is reproducible in principle.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture; no counterexample reported up to 10^18.

ai.disclosed_cost: About two weeks on a 'medium setup' (no hardware detail given).

events.what_happened: Pomerance and Weingartner, 'Exceptions to the Erdős-Straus-Schinzel conjecture' (arXiv:2511.16817, v1 20 Nov 2025, v2 15 Jan 2026). Schinzel conjectured that for each m ≥ 4 there is a bound beyond which m/n is a sum of three unit fractions. The paper shows that if such a bound exists it must be at least exp(m^(1/3 + o(1))). Explicitly, for m ≥ 6.52 × 10^9 there is a prime p in (m², 2m²) with m/p not such a sum. Numerical evidence is given for m ≥ 20, and the m = 5 case is checked to 10^18.
events.revisions: v1 20 Nov 2025; v2 15 Jan 2026 (current; 25 pages, 1 table).
events.delivers: Results for large m: failures of Schinzel's bound for arbitrarily large n, and an explicit prime failure for m ≥ 6.52 × 10^9. The abstract says nothing about m = 4. The m = 5 computation concerns the Sierpiński-type 5/n problem.
events.remains: The m = 4 case, which is the Erdős-Straus conjecture, is not addressed by these results.
events.direction: A different question (Schinzel's conjecture for large m); cuts against Schinzel's conjecture for large m, with no direction for m = 4.

events.what_happened: Lean 4 project 'erdstrau' (github.com/leochlon/erdstrau), announced by its author in an erdosproblems.com forum post of 27 Jan 2026. The post reports 531 formalised items, 484 complete, and sorry-free proofs for n = 420k + r with k odd and r in {121, 169, 289, 361}. It also says the full conjecture 'reduces to one construction'. A file posted by BorisAlexeev on 29 Jan 2026 claims 'Full CRT coverage' for n ≡ 529 (mod 840). The GitHub repository returned HTTP 404 when fetched.
events.revisions: Not established: repository unreachable at check time.
events.delivers: As claimed: formal proofs for the residue classes listed in the post. The 529 (mod 840) CRT file was judged by Thomas Bloom not to be a proof (see checked_by). Nothing here establishes the general case, which the post itself says is open.
events.remains: The general case, and every n outside the formalised classes.

checked_by.what_they_did: Replied on 29 Jan 2026 to the 529 (mod 840) file: 'this isn't actually a proof of anything.' He said the file checks only small n and appeals to periodicity, and that 'the statement is obviously not periodic.'

events.directly_checkable: The Lean files, if reachable. They were not reachable at check time.
events.doubts: Repository unreachable (404) at check time. The counts (531 items, 484 complete) and the sorry-free claims are unverified. Bloom's objection to the 529 file is recorded above.
events.direction: Partial formalisation; no direction on the general case.

events.what_happened: Bradford (unaffiliated), 'A solution to the Straus-Erdős conjecture' (arXiv:2602.11774, v1 only, 12 Feb 2026). Abstract, verbatim: 'This paper outlines a solution to the Straus Erdős Conjecture. Namely for each prime p there exists positive integers x ≤ y ≤ z so that' 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z. The argument splits solutions into Type I (p does not divide y) and Type II (p divides y), gives parametric families (Propositions 1 and 2, Lemmas 1 and 2) and residue classes mod 44, 20, 8 and 140, and ends by saying 'the last thing that we must show is that this is a covering system'. The erdosproblems.com forum records the claim on 13 Feb 2026.
events.revisions: v1 only (12 Feb 2026, 4 KB).
events.delivers: As claimed: for each prime p a three-term representation, which would settle the conjecture. As written, the parametric families are asserted per residue class, and the covering step is not carried out (per the extraction, 'The covering argument is never carried out'). At most the listed families are established.
events.remains: On the text as read: the covering of all primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4), which the paper leaves undone, and the identities it attributes to 'a previous paper'.

checked_by.what_they_did: Said the final sentence on the covering system 'seems to hint it is incorrect/ incomplete', that taking primes modulo different moduli does not create a covering system, and that none of Mordell's six residues mod 840 are excluded.

checked_by.who: ChatGPT Pro (shared chat that Terence Tao linked on 13 Feb 2026)
checked_by.qualification: AI critique, not a human reading
checked_by.what_they_did: Critique of this attempt. The shared page showed only its title ('ChatGPT - Paper critique request'); the content could not be retrieved, so its verdict is unknown.

checked_by.qualification: Expert in the area; did not evaluate this proof in the post
checked_by.what_they_did: Warned that the problem attracts many low-quality attempts and listed five conditions for trusting a new preprint (journal acceptance, track record, realistic partial results, expert vouching, formalisation). The thread reports none of them for this paper.

events.directly_checkable: For a given prime, the stated families can be checked by hand. The covering claim for primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) is the step that would need checking.
events.doubts: (1) The text calls itself an outline and says 'The last thing that we must show is that this is a covering system' without showing it. (2) The Type I identity 4xy − (x+y)p = gcd(xy, x+y) is taken from 'a previous paper' and not reproduced. (3) The Type II bound x ≥ ⌈p/4⌉ is called 'trivial' without argument. (4) The text states that 5, 13, 17, 29 are 'the first four primes that are 11 modulo 44'. They are not: 5, 13, 17 and 29 are not ≡ 11 (mod 44), and every number ≡ 11 (mod 44) other than 11 itself is a multiple of 11. (5) Mordell's residues mod 840 (including 169, the class of 1009) are not shown excluded, per the forum. (6) The forum records the gap report from StijnC, above. A 'research log' on artificialanalysis.ai (a model-evaluation site, low reliability) says the families are valid but no global covering is given; that is not an independent check.
events.direction: Claims a proof of the conjecture for all primes, which would settle it. The text describes itself as an outline.

events.what_happened: Mballa, 'A unified parametric approach to the Erdős-Straus conjecture with explicit solutions for a set of integers of natural density one' (arXiv:2602.20036, sole author, v1 23 Feb 2026, v2 22 Mar 2026). Claims explicit symmetric solutions (y = z) for n ≡ 0, 2, 3 (mod 4), 'covering already 75% of all integers' (abstract), and for n ≡ 1 (mod 4) when there is a divisor b ≡ 3 (mod 4). The abstract says the exceptions have natural density zero and that the conjecture is 'verified for a proportion of integers tending to 1' in this class.
events.revisions: v1 23 Feb 2026 (10 KB); v2 22 Mar 2026 (10 KB, current).
events.delivers: Explicit solutions for n ≡ 0, 2, 3 (mod 4) and for n ≡ 1 (mod 4) with a divisor b ≡ 3 (mod 4). The classes n ≡ 0, 2, 3 (mod 4) are classes the other sources already report as known (Ghermoul's page: confirmed for even a and for a ≡ 3 (mod 4)), so the new content is the n ≡ 1 (mod 4) part. A density-one statement does not decide existence for every n, since the abstract says the exceptions have density zero, not that they are empty.
events.remains: The density-zero exceptional set (not shown empty), in particular n ≡ 1 (mod 4) without a divisor b ≡ 3 (mod 4).
events.directly_checkable: Explicit symmetric solutions for given n can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Partial, toward the conjecture; density-one scope.

events.what_happened: Chamberland (Grinnell College), 'The Erdős-Straus Conjecture and the Structure of Primes', Integers 26 (2026), article A42. Per search snippets: received Oct 2025, accepted 25 Feb 2026, published April 2026. No arXiv version found. States that for a prime p, 4/p is a sum of three unit fractions with exactly two denominators divisible by p if and only if p = qr − 4 s1 s2 with q ≡ 3 (mod 4) and s1, s2 divisors of (q + 1)/4. States a 'Prime Representation Conjecture' that every prime has this form; the paper does not claim to prove it.
events.revisions: No arXiv version found. The journal publication month (April 2026) is the earliest public appearance I found.
events.delivers: A characterisation, for primes p, of one type of solution, conditional on p having the stated form. It does not decide the conjecture for any p outside that form.
events.remains: Every prime not of the stated form, and the Prime Representation Conjecture that all primes are of that form.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted 25 Feb 2026 and published April 2026, per search snippets; the PDF was not parseable

events.directly_checkable: For a given prime p the stated characterisation can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Partial characterisation; the all-primes version is conjectural and open.

events.what_happened: Ventas, 'A Ceiling Continued Fraction Approach to the Erdős-Straus Conjecture: Heuristic finiteness of counterexamples' (arXiv:2605.04551, v1 6 May 2026, v2 25 May 2026, 10 pages). Introduces a 'ceiling continued fraction' framework that uses divisors of p + i rather than congruences. Derives a super-polynomial bound on the failure probability and argues, via Borel-Cantelli, that counterexamples, if any exist, are heuristically finite. Computational tests on 10^9 primes near 10^17, 10^52 and 10^131 with very small search depth found none.
events.revisions: v1 6 May 2026; v2 25 May 2026 (current).
events.delivers: Heuristic only, by the abstract's own wording ('provides heuristic evidence'). The computations are finite and cover 10^9 primes at three scales, which moves no quantity the problem asks for.
events.remains: Everything: no existence proof for any prime or any n.
events.doubts: The finiteness argument is heuristic on the paper's own terms, and the computations use very small search depth (per the abstract).
events.direction: Heuristic evidence toward the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Bello-Hernández, Benito and Fernández, 'A Divisor Parametrization for the Erdős-Strauss Conjecture' (arXiv:2606.10922, v1 9 Jun 2026, 15 pages). Defines fab(n, a, b) from divisors, whose admissible parameters recover the decompositions of 1/n with all three denominators divisible by 4. For m = 4, the text's Theorem 5 (per the HTML extraction) proves that if n ≡ 1 (mod 4) and 1/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with 4 | x, y, z, then some admissible parameters reproduce that decomposition. Remark 6 notes that fab(n, a, b) may be smaller than the k used in the proof, so the abstract's 'exactly recovers' is established in one direction only.
events.revisions: v1 only (9 Jun 2026).
events.delivers: A parametrization of the sub-family of Erdős-Straus decompositions in which the denominators are multiples of 4 (equivalently, the triples with this divisibility), in one direction. It does not show that a decomposition exists for any given n.
events.remains: Existence for each n, and decompositions outside the 4-divisible family.
events.doubts: The abstract's 'exactly recovers' claim is one-directional in the text as extracted (Remark 6).
events.direction: Partial structural result; no direction on existence.

events.what_happened: Mohammad W. Alomari, 'A Simple Direct Proof of the Erdös-Straus Conjecture' (Authorea preprint, doi 10.22541/au.167569747.72416313). Its abstract, seen in a search snippet, says the conjecture holds and that the Sierpiński conjecture follows. The page returned HTTP 403 when fetched, so the argument was not read. No posting date was found.
events.revisions: Not established.
events.delivers: Claimed full proof of the conjecture (per the abstract). Not verified.
events.remains: Unknown: argument not read.
events.doubts: Argument not read; posting date unknown; Authorea hosts unrefereed preprints; I found no endorsement or refutation.
events.direction: Claims a full resolution (unverified).

events.what_happened: Shang Yu Chen, 'The Erdős-Straus Conjecture: Modulo 24 Obstructions and the Constant Residual Constraint' (Cambridge Open Engage, working paper; v1 3 Aug 2026, v2 27 Aug 2026). The abstract, verbatim in parts: 'By decomposing the Erdős-Straus equation into four simultaneous algebraic-analytic systems, we obtain an absolute residual constant that strictly bounds all admissible solutions. This constraint resolves the intrinsic modulo 24 obstruction and reduces the Diophantine problem to a finite, computable domain.' The page shows no affiliation and states it has not been peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press.
events.revisions: v1 3 Aug 2026; v2 27 Aug 2026. The v2 notes mention 'the referee's comments' with no content on the page.
events.delivers: As claimed: a reduction of the whole problem to a finite computable domain, which would be a full resolution. The page gives no argument, residue class or prime, so nothing it establishes can be read from the page.
events.remains: Cannot be determined from the posted abstract.
events.doubts: No argument on the page. No affiliation is shown. Not peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press. The v2 notes mention a referee's comments with no content.
events.direction: Claims a full resolution (unverified).

events.what_happened: Dahan, 'Sieve dimension and search depth for the Erdős-Straus conjecture, n ≡ 1 (mod 24)' (arXiv:2608.24035, v1 25 Aug 2026). Per the abstract: unconditional bounds on exceptional sets of primes for every fixed J; an obstruction at the shift c = 7, so a fixed shift cannot leave a finite residual set; and a factorization-free procedure that decides the conjecture for all primes in an interval [N, 2N]. The abstract states that 'the conjecture itself remains open.'
events.revisions: v1 only (25 Aug 2026, 57 KB).
events.delivers: Restricted to primes in the class n ≡ 1 (mod 24). It gives a computational decision for primes in each interval [N, 2N], which is a finite instance set and moves no count. It also gives an unconditional bound on exceptional sets, which may count the potential exceptions; that is flagged for judgement. The c = 7 obstruction is negative for one method.
events.remains: The conjecture for all primes, including primes outside the n ≡ 1 (mod 24) class and beyond the intervals decided.
events.direction: Partial, toward the conjecture for a subclass; no decision for all primes.

events.what_happened: Jiang, 'Counting Type I and Type II solutions of the Erdos-Straus equation: concentration, local obstructions, and a pointwise comparison' (arXiv:2609.09204). v1 5 Sep 2026; v2 13 Sep 2026, now withdrawn by the author. The abstract says 'We do not address the Erdos-Straus conjecture itself', proves an unconditional bound on Type II solutions, and conjectures f_I(p) > f_II(p) for p > 5, p not ≡ 1 (mod 8), with numerical support to p ≤ 10^6. The comments field reads '_some errors_'.
events.revisions: v1 5 Sep 2026; v2 13 Sep 2026, withdrawn by the author.
events.delivers: Nothing on existence: the paper says it does not address the conjecture. Its counting bounds are withdrawn.
events.remains: Everything.
events.doubts: Withdrawn by the author, and its comments field flags errors.

withdrawn.what: The whole paper, arXiv:2609.09204 (v2 of 13 Sep 2026 is marked withdrawn; the comments field reads '_some errors_').

events.direction: Not about existence; a counting result, now withdrawn.

disputes.summary: Bradford (12 Feb 2026) claims a proof for every prime; the forum records a gap report (StijnC, 13 Feb 2026) that the covering step does not exclude Mordell's residues mod 840. Unresolved in every source found.

Dyachenko (7 Nov 2025): the abstract states a representation for every prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4). The Conclusion as extracted says the infinite-family case is not proven constructively and that Appendix D's steps are conditional. These readings are not reconciled in any source found.

Mballa's perfect-square conjecture: Bouamoud's Dec 2025 preprint argues the polynomial fails to give a square for n = 3; Bouamoud's Jan 2026 preprint claims it always does for n ≥ 2. The two contradict each other; neither is refereed.
Mordell's date is given as 1967 (Wikipedia) and as Mo68 and Mo69 on erdosproblems.com. Not a dispute about the mathematics; recorded because the year is uncertain.

summary: Searched 48 queries across the problem's names, its residue-class and computational history, the claimed proofs, the forum and wiki for the problem, and AI names and AI-result trackers, and opened about 35 sources (listed below, with opened flags). No resolution, no counterexample, and no claimed proof has been accepted by a reader I could identify. The problem is still listed as open on erdosproblems.com (page last edited 7 May 2026; the forum comments run to Feb 2026 and posting is shown as suspended) and on Wikipedia (edited 3 Aug 2026). Since Jan 2024 the record holds: a computational extension to 10^18 (Mihnea and Dumitru, Aug 2025, an unrefereed preprint calling itself empirical evidence); several partial or conjectural frameworks (Lopez 2024; Bradford 2024, published in Integers 2025 as an equivalence with a conjectured existence statement; Ghermoul 2025 for a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and the 5/a variant; Schuh 2025; Mballa 2025 and 2026; Chamberland, Integers 2026, a characterisation for primes of a stated form; Ventas 2026, heuristic only; Bello-Hernández et al. 2026, a divisor parametrisation in one direction; Dahan 2026, the class n ≡ 1 (mod 24) with a computational decision on intervals; Pomerance and Weingartner 2025, which concerns Schinzel's m/n for large m and says nothing about m = 4); and three claims of a full or prime-case proof: Dyachenko (Nov 2025; for every prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4); if it held, it would settle the problem with the standard reduction and the 3 mod 4 identity, which I derived myself; the paper's Conclusion, as extracted, limits what is proved, so the scope is open), Bradford (Feb 2026; an outline whose covering step is not carried out and which the forum reader flagged as incomplete), and Chen (Aug 2026; abstract only, no argument on the page). Alomari's undated Authorea claim was not readable (403). Jiang's Sept 2026 paper is withdrawn and does not address the conjecture. AI: no source credits an AI system with any of the mathematics on this problem. The AI-related items I found are: (i) Bello-Hernández, Benito and Fernández (arXiv 2606.10922), whose Acknowledgments and AI Tool Disclosure reads 'ChatGPT 5.5 was used for proofreading. Outside of this AI tool use, the mathematics and the text of this paper were both human-generated.' This is proofreading only, so it is not in ai.systems; (ii) Dyachenko's acknowledgements thank 'various AI models for assistance in refining explanations, proofreading' and 'creating illustrative Python examples' (per the extraction). No model is named, and the author describes no load-bearing role, so ai.systems is empty; (iii) a ChatGPT Pro critique of Bradford's attempt, linked by Terence Tao on 13 Feb 2026. Its content could not be retrieved, and it is a critic, not a credited contributor. Tao's AI-contributions wiki (last updated 30 Jun 2026) has no entry for problem 242 or Straus; the 2026 AI Erdős results I found (OpenAI's unit-distance disproof, GPT-5.2 Pro on #281 and #728, DeepMind's Aletheia and AlphaProof Nexus) concern other problems; the FrontierMath Erdős abstract (Sep 2026) does not list this problem in the text I could read; Quanta's 3 Aug 2026 AI article does not mention it. Close calls: (a) whether Dyachenko's Theorem 10.21 is a uniform existence proof for all primes ≡ 1 (mod 4), or only an explicit construction plus a per-prime existence argument, which is how I read the Conclusion; (b) whether Bradford's covering step can be completed; (c) the forum's 18 Nov 2025 remark that 'two papers' claim full or almost complete proofs, one called 'very mistaken', which I could not tie to a specific preprint; (d) whether Vaughan's exception bound counts all n or only primes; (e) the statement's wording: the Wikipedia form allows non-distinct triples and n ≥ 2, while erdosproblems.com requires distinct x < y < z and n > 2, which differ only at n = 2, and this record follows the Wikipedia wording.
competing_reading: Take Dyachenko's abstract at face value. It asserts a representation for every prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4). Together with the identity for primes ≡ 3 (mod 4), p = 2, and the standard scaling reduction, that would settle the conjecture. On that reading the Conclusion's words ('not proven constructively' for infinite families, Appendix D 'conditional') concern explicitness or the method's uniformity rather than existence for each prime, and the result is a full proof by an unaffiliated author that nobody has yet checked. The opposing reading takes the Conclusion as the author's own limit on what is proved, so the claim is at most per-prime and conditional for the infinite family. The ES conjecture's status as open rests on the second reading, since no one I found has checked the first.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report or expert note on Dyachenko's Theorem 10.21 and on the Appendix D steps that use Dirichlet's theorem and finite coverings, in particular whether existence is shown for every prime P ≡ 1 (mod 4) or only for each prime by a conditional argument. (2) For Bradford, either a completed covering argument for all primes ≡ 1 (mod 4), or a reader's identification of a specific uncovered class (the forum has already raised Mordell's residues mod 840). (3) The full text of Chen's Cambridge posting, including whether v2 has any argument. (4) A working copy of the leochlon/erdstrau repository (it returned 404), with its sorry count and whether any AI system wrote its Lean code. (5) A change on erdosproblems.com/242 or in Tao's AI-contributions wiki for this problem. (6) The full text of arXiv 2606.10922 (proofreading statement and Theorem 5, read in HTML) and the Chamberland and Bradford Integers PDFs (not parseable here). (7) The primaries for Obláth 1950, Swett 1999, Mordell 1967 to 1969 and Vaughan 1970, to fix the dates and the quantity Vaughan's bound counts. (8) Alomari's Authorea PDF and its posting date.
